# Q227 — Why a rule-bearing bus with unversioned "services" is not SOA

## 0. Onboarding and scope

I ran describe first with --volume atlas. The returned contract reports snapshot 4445fa068e7a0392182bb996f9e6c6dcd4dc0bdb6dd991fec215d020f2f8e04a, route snapshot 11c139259bd03a3a193b068b0d52a36474fdbec547394d60b76cc32d2eecd742, 555 documents, 3,132 sections, and a draft pattern registry 0.2.0 with 145 entries (86 sufficient, 48 partial, 11 partial-bounded). The atlas layer is primary because the question is an atlas applicability judgment; the book layer supplies the contract mechanism and the owner pages behind the cards. The modeling-and-simulation layer is not needed: no model, run, scenario or accepted decision is at issue, and the question asks for an architectural classification, not a simulation result. I searched atlas and book with three or more formulations per facet; the facet matrix and the session log record the trail.

Saturation note: after the first pass, later formulations returned the same cards and owner sections. "mediation layer" returned only the SOA card; "canonical data model" returned a CQRS page, not a separate canonical-model card; "consumer-driven contract compatibility" returned only a proposed-structure landing. Two consecutive rounds added no new evidence. The remaining gaps are facts about the hypothetical program (ownership, deployment, whether the bus mappings are owned), not missing source text, so I preserve them in section 6 rather than fill them.

## 2. Direct answer

The atlas rejects the claim that this program is service-oriented architecture, not service orientation as a style. The SOA card is applicable-under-conditions: it applies when independently governed services and contracts are composed across organizational boundaries, with explicit contracts and mediation, governed lifecycle and versioning, and an organization that accepts integration overhead. The card's hard contraindications say to reject the claim for one team and one deployable, when no service governance exists, when SOA is used as a synonym for an enterprise bus, and when contracts cannot be versioned and owned. The described program exhibits at least three of those four conditions: the bus is the integration story; no capability can name a contract version; no capability can name a consumer; and governance is therefore absent. The fourth condition, one team and one deployable, is not established by the premise and must be checked, because if it holds, the honest comparison is a modular monolith rather than SOA.

"Every integration is a service" is taxonomy inflation. In atlas terms a service is a published capability with an interaction contract and an owner, not a route, adapter or subscription on a bus. An endpoint does not establish ownership, and a matching pattern name is not evidence of fit. Once the bus performs transformation and business rules, the effective contract is the bus mapping, not the nominal service. Authority is displaced from the capability owner to a central component, the contract identifies no parties whose obligations it governs, and the architecture relies on the enterprise-service-bus pattern: Microsoft reports large central brokers and ESBs as typical SOA features and, in most cases, anti-patterns in the microservices community, while Fowler and Lewis describe ESB products as including routing, choreography, transformation and business rules. It is also a shared bottleneck and single point of failure, and one canonical model can hide contextual differences between domains.

A governed service contract must declare, at minimum: the capability and the real-world effect it produces; who may invoke it, under which trust and tenant context and policies; the identity and meaning of commands, state and errors; protocol and schema versions, supported lifecycle and deprecation; the supported consumer set and each consumer's obligations; deadlines, idempotency scope and uncertain outcomes; consistency and freshness, published events and replay behavior; the failure mode when the service is unreachable; and who owns the operation, data protection and consumer compatibility. Schema alone is not a contract: an OpenAPI document or protobuf file declares message formats, not domain semantics, effect authority or tolerance for meaning-changing changes. OASIS supplies the anchor: a service contract is a measurable assertion governing the requirements and expectations of two or more parties, and a consumer needs the function, the applicable policies and constraints, and the format, content and expected sequences of information exchange. Tycho's synthesis adds that capability, message semantics, version and consumer obligations are mandatory metadata, backed by a maintained consumer inventory.

Microservices is the better comparison only when multiple teams need independent release cadence, capabilities have separate scaling or failure-isolation needs, automation, observability and contract testing exist, data ownership can be separated, and the organization accepts network and consistency costs. It is the wrong comparison for one small team with a shared release cadence, no operational platform, unavoidable cross-service transactions or shared authoritative data. A service count is not evidence of autonomy, and a service that cannot name a version or a consumer would not thereby become a microservice if it were put in its own process; the independence test would still fail, and the common result is the distributed monolith the owner page warns about.

A modular monolith is the better comparison when one accountable owner or a small group has a shared release cadence, module contracts and data ownership can be enforced by build or review checks, local transactions are valuable, and independent runtime scaling or failure isolation is not yet required. It is not a license for shared tables and unowned internals: the atlas counterexample is exactly a one-unit deployment with shared tables and no enforceable module contract. If the described program is one deployable for one team, the central bus can at most be an internal mediator; its transformations and business rules still need module owners and enforceable module APIs, or the program remains an unstructured monolith with a rule engine in the middle.

## 3. Mechanism and justification

### 3.1 A service is a governed capability, not an integration endpoint (F1)

The SOA card's decision question is whether independently governed services and contracts should be composed across organizational boundaries, rather than designed as one application or one microservice estate. Its good-fit conditions require heterogeneous systems with separate governance, explicit contracts and mediation, integration that spans ownership boundaries, a service lifecycle and versioning that can be governed, and an organization that accepts integration overhead. The owner page adds the source definition: SOA is "a paradigm for organizing and utilizing distributed capabilities that may be under the control of different ownership domains" (OASIS §2.1), and a service is a published capability with an interaction contract. The book's four-axis analysis is the same point in another form: business/domain boundary, code/module boundary, runtime/deployment boundary and data ownership are separate decisions. The named shortcuts are treating every database table or REST endpoint as a bounded context and assuming a separate process establishes a good domain boundary; I would add the inverse shortcut in the premise: assuming every integration is a service because it is called one.

This matters because the label carries obligations. A capability label asserts an owner, a describable effect, a boundary that can change independently, and a contract that someone can rely on. If none of those can be named, the word "service" is doing no architectural work; it is a diagram convention. The atlas chapter is explicit that "a matching name or a passing structural check is not evidence that a pattern fits a workload", and gives the shared-table monolith as its counterexample. The same standard applies to a bus with many "services" attached: the topology does not prove the pattern.

### 3.2 The claim fails the card's hard contraindications (F2)

The card lists four hard contraindications, and the premise maps to them as follows:

| Contraindication | Premise | Status |
|---|---|---|
| One team and one deployable | Not stated; a "program" may be one deployable or several | Unknown |
| No service governance exists | No capability can name a contract version or a consumer; no evidence of ownership, lifecycle or compatibility policy | Triggered |
| SOA used as a synonym for an enterprise bus | All calls route through one central bus that applies transformations and business rules | Triggered |
| Contracts cannot be versioned and owned | No contract version is nameable for any capability; ownership is not established | Triggered |

The card text is observed; the premise-to-contraindication mapping is my inference. That is not a borderline fit. It is the condition the card says to reject, and the decision state applicable-under-conditions does not rescue it: the conditions are precisely what is missing. This is also why the atlas is not rejecting SOA as such. The card remains a valid comparison for a different system: one with genuinely independent owners, governed contracts, and mediation as a real, owned capability. The rejection is of the label applied to this system, and of the implicit claim that a bus plus many endpoints satisfies the pattern.

### 3.3 Why a rule-bearing central bus is the wrong center (F3)

Mediation is not the problem. The SOA owner page says SOA publishes capabilities as governed service contracts and routes consumers through a mediation layer, and that "the bus is one implementation of that mediation, not the source of ownership." A bus can be a legitimate transport and routing choice. What fails is making the bus the place where meaning is decided.

The card records the relevant failure pattern. Microsoft reports that "large central brokers, central orchestrators at the organization level, and the Enterprise Service Bus (ESB)" are typical SOA features, and that "in most cases, these are anti-patterns in the microservice community." Fowler and Lewis observe that ESB products "often include sophisticated facilities for message routing, choreography, transformation, and applying business rules." Tycho synthesis: a centralized bus is a shared bottleneck and a single point that must be sized and failed over, with an observed fallback path that does not depend on it. The sources do not give a timeout, recovery bound or failover procedure.

The architectural consequence is more damaging than the operational one. If the bus transforms messages and applies business rules, then the bus, not the capability owner, decides what a message means and what effect follows. The nominal service contract ceases to describe the effective interface: its consumer cannot know the semantics without reading the bus configuration, and the bus becomes a second, unowned domain model. This displacement is my inference from the ownership definition and the anti-corruption-layer contraindications, not a direct quotation. The service-independence comparison table names the related hazard directly: "One global canonical model may hide contextual differences", and "An endpoint does not establish ownership." Two writers for one invariant remain unsafe no matter how the calls are routed. A consumer inventory and version policy cannot be maintained per capability when the compatibility surface is a shared mapping that changes for everyone at once.

Transformation is legitimate at a boundary when the semantics genuinely differ, the mapping and its errors are owned and tested, and the layer does not become a second domain model; those are the anti-corruption-layer conditions, and the card also warns that an ACL can become a single point of failure. Business rules belong with the capability that owns the invariant. Pipes and filters makes the same point about processing stages: compose stages only when each stage has an independent contract and the pipeline owns ordering, partial completion and recovery; otherwise keep one cohesive transformation. A central rule engine violates both qualifications: it is neither a boundary-local mapping with an owner nor a pipeline of independently contracted stages.

### 3.4 What a governed contract must declare (F4)

The owner page states the contract invariant: a service contract must declare its capability, message semantics, version and consumer obligations. It then quotes OASIS: a service contract is "a measurable assertion that governs the requirements and expectations of two or more parties" (§3.3.2.2), and a consumer needs to know that the service performs a certain function or set of functions, the applicable policies and constraints, and "the format and content of information exchanged between the service and the consumer and the sequences of information exchange that may be expected" (§3.3.1). The SOA reference model is technology-neutral; it does not prescribe an interface language, registry protocol, bus topology or service size.

The book's service-contract section turns that into an operational checklist. A useful contract must specify:

1. who is eligible to invoke which effect, with trust and tenant context;
2. the identity and meaning of commands, state and errors;
3. protocol and schema versions, supported lifecycle and deprecation;
4. operation deadlines, idempotency scope and uncertain outcomes;
5. consistency and freshness, published events and replay behavior;
6. the failure mode when the service is unreachable;
7. who owns operation, data protection and consumer compatibility.

It adds that an OpenAPI document or protobuf schema can declare message formats but does not by itself specify domain semantics or guarantee that consumers tolerate a meaning-changing enum update. The microservices owner note adds the same obligations from the independence side: each service publishes its contract, version policy and supported consumer set. Tycho's synthesis is that capability, message semantics, version and consumer obligations are mandatory contract metadata, with a maintained consumer inventory; the sources describe the content and the independence aim, not a contract schema.

The premise fails the version and consumer requirements directly. No capability can name a version, so lifecycle, deprecation and compatibility cannot be governed. No capability can name a consumer, so there is no party whose obligations can be specified and no compatibility impact to measure. What remains is an interface description at best, and often not even that. This is why the missing version and consumer are not bookkeeping gaps; they are the evidence that the contract does not exist in the sense SOA requires.

### 3.5 When microservices is the better comparison (F5)

The microservices card sets the fit conditions: multiple teams need independent release cadence; capabilities have separate scaling or failure-isolation needs; automation, observability and contract testing exist; data ownership can be separated; and the organization accepts network and consistency costs. Its hard contraindications are one small team with a shared release cadence, no operational platform, unavoidable cross-service transactions, or shared authoritative data. It also states the diagnostic that matters here: "A service count is not evidence of autonomy."

The owner page makes independence concrete. A microservice owner accepts a deployable, its data and the pager that follows both; independence is credible only when the team can release without coordinating another service's schedule. Each service publishes its contract, version policy and supported consumer set. Shared tables, hidden synchronous chains and lockstep migrations undermine the boundary regardless of repository layout, and a shared client library does not make contract changes independent. The book's comparison table adds that neither style is automatically more resilient or scalable: a microservice architecture with synchronous, chatty calls can amplify timeouts, and a replicated monolith with strong cache and data design may serve substantial traffic.

So microservices is the right comparison when the question is which capabilities need independent deployment, failure containment, state ownership and life cycles strongly enough to justify remote cost. It is not the right comparison merely because the current integration is ugly or the bus is central. If the described program cannot name versions or consumers, splitting it into processes would reproduce the same missing contract at a higher cost: that is the distributed-monolith failure the owner page warns about. The comparison becomes live only after ownership, release cadence and data authority are named and measured.

### 3.6 When a modular monolith is the better comparison (F6)

The modular-monolith card sets the other side: the capability has one accountable owner or a small group with a shared release cadence; module contracts and data ownership can be enforced by build or review checks; local transactions are valuable; independent runtime scaling or failure isolation is not yet required. Its contraindications are equally explicit: reject when modules need independent deployment, scaling or failure isolation; when no team can enforce boundary ownership; when a regulatory or trust boundary requires separate runtime isolation; or when "modular" describes shared tables with no enforced contract.

The book's four-axis analysis and the modular-monolith worked example make the same distinction. A monolith can be a single deployment unit and still contain well-separated modules with explicit internal APIs; the defining cost is shared deployment and shared runtime exposure, not an absence of contracts. The atlas counterexample is a one-unit deployment with shared tables and no enforceable module contract, which is not evidence for the card. The decision record on modular-first is consistent but must be read with its own caveat: it is an original analytical draft with reviewer pending and unknown evidence status, and it says to prefer a modular monolith first only for its synthetic case, to extract a service only when independent release, failure or scaling needs are real, and not to split when the only problem is ungoverned package dependencies.

For the described program, the modular monolith is the better comparison if it is one deployable for one team. The central bus could then be an internal mediator, but the transformations and business rules still need owners inside the modules, and the module APIs still need versioning and consumer identification if anything outside the module calls them. If the integrations genuinely cross independent ownership domains, the modular monolith is the wrong frame and the question returns to SOA governance or microservices, depending on whether independence is real.

### 3.7 The residual valid SOA

The atlas does not leave SOA without a domain. The owner page says SOA is a fit when many independent owners must integrate through stable contracts and mediation is a real, owned capability. The card's good-fit conditions say the same: heterogeneous systems with separate governance, explicit contracts and mediation, integration across ownership boundaries, governed lifecycle and versioning, and acceptance of integration overhead. The bus is optional in that description; it is one mediation implementation, and the reference model does not mandate it. The card also says to reverse the choice when governance and mediation overhead exceeds the integration benefit, and the owner page notes that some microservice advocates reject the SOA label entirely while others see microservices as one form of SOA.

That residual matters for the answer's boundary. If the program actually has independent owners behind the integrations, stable contracts that can be versioned, named consumers, and a mediation capability with its own owner, then the same central bus might be acceptable mediation even though the current documentation is inadequate. The atlas would still demand that the contracts and consumer inventory be made explicit, and it would still question business rules living in the bus. The rejection is conditional on the facts stated, and the facts stated are exactly the ones the card treats as disqualifying.

## 4. Boundaries and trade-offs

- Mediation is not banned. The card's good-fit conditions include explicit mediation, and the owner page treats the bus as one implementation. A routing bus with boundary-owned translations can be legitimate. The failure is bus-as-owner and bus-as-definition.
- Transformation is not banned. Semantic translation at an owned boundary is the anti-corruption layer's purpose. The card rejects it when the models already align, when it adds no semantic translation, when it has no owner, or when it becomes a second domain model. Those conditions are the test for the bus's transformations too.
- Microservices is not the automatic alternative. The card's contraindications cover the common case where distribution makes things worse. A service count is not autonomy, and separate processes with shared tables and lockstep releases are a distributed monolith.
- A modular monolith is not contract-free. The card requires enforceable module contracts and data ownership; shared tables with no contract are its counterexample. An internal bus does not substitute for module APIs.
- SOA is not obsolete. The card is applicable-under-conditions and remains a fit for many independent owners with stable contracts and owned mediation. The answer rejects a label, not a style.
- The evidence is decision guidance, not production proof. The atlas chapter says no entry claims sufficient technical or decision coverage, and no independent review, benchmark, production observation or runtime test is asserted. The registry is draft (describe metadata). The sources (OASIS, Microsoft guidance, Fowler/Lewis) are descriptive or definitional, not comparative measurements. The decision record used for the modular-first boundary is an analytical draft with unknown evidence status.
- The answer does not hold if the premise is incomplete in specific ways: if named consumers and versions exist but are undocumented; if the bus only routes and its transformations are boundary-owned mappings; if the "business rules" are routing policy rather than domain invariants; or if the integrations cross independent ownership domains with real governance. Each of those would move the judgment, and section 6 says what evidence would settle it.

## 6. Unknowns and confidence

Unknowns that materially change the answer:

1. Team and deployment topology. If the program is one team and one deployable, the modular monolith is the better comparison and the SOA label is wrong for an additional reason. If it is several independently released services, the distributed-monolith critique applies.
2. Ownership of the integrations. If the integrations cross genuinely independent ownership domains, the SOA question becomes legitimate once contracts exist. If they are all inside one domain, the service framing is decorative.
3. The status of the bus mappings. If the transformations are boundary-owned, tested ACLs and the bus only routes, the conclusion softens. If they are central business rules, the ESB critique is direct.
4. Whether consumers and versions exist but are undocumented. The premise says they cannot be named; if that is a documentation failure rather than an architectural one, the remedy is governance, not necessarily a style change.
5. Whether "business rules" means routing policy or domain invariants. Routing policy in a bus is an operational choice; domain invariants in a bus are an ownership violation.
6. Measurements. No release lead time, blast radius, scaling evidence, failure isolation or operating cost is given, and the atlas itself asserts no production observation. Any microservices-versus-monolith recommendation without those measurements is a hypothesis.

Confidence: high that the described program fails the SOA card's contraindications and the contract invariant as stated; high that a contract must declare version, consumers, semantics, policies, failure behavior and ownership; medium on the precise architectural verdict because ownership and deployment facts are missing; low on any recommendation between microservices and modular monolith without measurement. The answer would change most if evidence showed independent owners with governed, versioned contracts behind the bus, or one team and one deployable with a shared release cadence.

evidence.claim: A useful contract specifies eligibility/trust/tenant context, command/state/error meaning, protocol and schema versions with lifecycle and deprecation, deadlines/idempotency/uncertain outcomes, consistency/freshness/events/replay, failure mode, and ownership of operation/data protection/consumer compatibility; schema alone is insufficient.
evidence.note: Observed. The seven-bullet list is on the page; the OpenAPI/protobuf caveat is explicit.

evidence.claim: Microservices fit requires multiple teams with independent release cadence, separate scaling or failure isolation, automation/observability/contract testing, separable data ownership and acceptance of network/consistency costs; one small team, no platform, unavoidable cross-service transactions or shared authoritative data are contraindications; service count is not autonomy.
evidence.note: Observed. The card's good-fit and hard-contraindication sections, including the sentence 'A service count is not evidence of autonomy.'

evidence.claim: Microservice independence is credible only when the team can release without coordinating another service's schedule; each service publishes its contract, version policy and supported consumer set; shared tables, hidden synchronous chains and lockstep migrations undermine the boundary.
evidence.note: Observed Tycho guidance in the Microservices Architecture ownership note. The page labels the release-independence reasoning as guidance, not a measured result.

evidence.claim: Modular monolith fit requires one accountable owner or small group with shared cadence, enforceable module contracts and data ownership, valuable local transactions, and no current need for independent scaling or failure isolation; shared tables without enforced contract are contraindicated.
evidence.note: Observed. The card's good-fit, hard-contraindication and competing-alternative sections. The card's failure section describes the distributed monolith in disguise: shared data, synchronous call chains and one deployment blast radius.

evidence.claim: An endpoint does not establish ownership; one global canonical model may hide contextual differences; two writers for one invariant remain unsafe; coordinated schema deployment can defeat independence.
evidence.note: Observed. The service-oriented versus microservice-style comparison table states these cautions directly.

evidence.claim: A separate container does not prove independence; shared tables, imported internal structures, meaning-changing events without consumer compatibility, shared release gates and missing operational ownership all recreate lockstep coupling.
evidence.note: Observed. The page also says distinct modules in one executable may be safer when local transactions matter and independent release brings little benefit.

evidence.claim: Distribution is justified by a cohesive capability with an externally clear contract, an established team, materially independent release pressure and validated benefit above cost; unstable boundaries, chatty calls, local-transaction invariants, scarce operations and no proven need argue against it; neither style is automatically resilient or scalable.
evidence.note: Observed page synthesis. The page calls monolith-first a hypothesis or strategy and reports that Fowler's evidence was anecdotal.

evidence.claim: Domain, code/module, runtime/deployment and data ownership are separate axes; treating every table or REST endpoint as a bounded context, and assuming a process establishes a domain boundary, are named shortcuts.
evidence.note: Observed. The four-axis table and the surrounding definition of a service are on the page.

evidence.claim: A monolithic application can be one deployment unit while containing well-separated functional modules with explicit internal APIs; the defining cost is shared deployment and runtime failure exposure, not an inability to implement contracts.
evidence.note: Observed. The section says a monolith can still contain well-separated modules and that shared deployment and process/runtime failure exposure are the defining costs, not missing interfaces or contracts.

evidence.claim: A modular monolith and independently deployable services differ on encapsulation, call path, independent release, atomic state change, failure/performance, operating cost, ownership and scale; neither is automatically more resilient or scalable.
evidence.note: Observed. The comparison table and the immediate sentence that neither style is automatically more resilient or scalable.

evidence.claim: Boundary translation is legitimate only when semantics genuinely differ, the mapping and its errors can be owned and tested, and the layer does not become a second domain model; an ACL can become a single point of failure.
evidence.note: Observed. The Anti-Corruption Layer card's good-fit, contraindication and failure sections.

evidence.claim: Processing stages should be composed only when each stage has an independent contract and the pipeline owns ordering, partial completion and recovery; otherwise keep one cohesive transformation, and stage retries or replays must be idempotent.
evidence.note: Observed. The page's decision, invariant and failure sections; the underlying source is a 2003 chapter, and the idempotency/backpressure/partial-completion guidance is labelled Tycho synthesis.

evidence.claim: SOA remains a fit when many independent owners must integrate through stable contracts and mediation is a real, owned capability; microservices may be preferable for independent product teams, and a modular monolith when one ownership boundary suffices.
evidence.note: Observed. The owner page's alternative paragraph is labelled Tycho synthesis; it also notes that some advocates reject the SOA label while others see microservices as one form of SOA.

evidence.claim: A remote boundary should be justified through independent ownership or deployment needs while accounting for communication and recovery costs; separate containers can still require synchronized releases and share one fragile datastore, so deployment count does not demonstrate independence.
evidence.note: Observed. The integrated decision section states the justification and the deployment-count counterpoint.

evidence.claim: Modular-first is a proposed ADR for a synthetic case with reversal triggers and unknown evidence status; it should not be generalized when teams can operate services, and splitting is not justified when the only problem is ungoverned package dependencies.
evidence.note: Observed with caveat. The decision record declares 'original analytical draft, independent reviewer pending' and evidence_status unknown; the ADR is explicitly proposed, not historical.

evidence.claim: Atlas coverage is decision guidance, not proof: no entry claims sufficient technical or decision coverage and no independent review, benchmark, production observation or runtime test is asserted.
evidence.note: Observed. The chapter landing's evidence limits also state that eight owner links are bounded sections rather than dedicated pages.
